title: Milk and blood
hook: tradition says he squeezed Lalo's bread and milk ran out, and from Bhago's feast, blood

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Lalo's bread, and a feast turned down. Your line was honest bread is sweet. What did you eat that someone honestly earned? Day thirty-four.

We left the story in a tense room. Malik Bhago, the rich official of Saidpur, has summoned Guru Nanak to explain himself. Why did you eat a carpenter's coarse bread and snub my feast? The townspeople have crowded in. Everyone wants to see what happens when a holy man with nothing insults a man with everything. And this is where the story, as tradition tells it, stops being a dinner-party drama and becomes something stranger. Nanak asks for two things to be brought: a piece of Lalo's bread, and a piece of food from Bhago's table. He takes one in each hand. Today, what happened when he squeezed.
screen: `A TENSE ROOM IN SAIDPUR.` → `ONE PIECE FROM EACH TABLE.` → `ONE IN EACH HAND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says he pressed them. From Lalo's bread, milk ran out. From Bhago's rich food, blood. That's the whole scene, and it's told in gurdwaras and in children's books and painted on walls. Sikhs read it in more than one way. Many take it as a miracle that really happened, a sign given to a proud man. Others read it as a picture, a parable in the language of the janamsakhis, which are full of wonders. And it's worth saying plainly: the milk and the blood don't appear in the scripture itself. They come from the later life stories. What the scripture does have is the idea underneath, in Guru Nanak's own words. In one hymn, he says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork is to a Muslim and beef is to a Hindu. Notice how he says it. He reaches for the one thing each of his neighbors would never eat, and says: that's what stolen wealth is. So in either reading, miracle or picture, the point is the same. Food carries its history. Lalo's bread came from sweat, and it's nourishing, like milk. Bhago's feast came from taxes and bribes and squeezing people who had little, and so, in the story's startling picture, it's made of their blood. Nobody could see it on the plate. The story makes it visible. And it asks a question that doesn't expire: not how much do you have, or how nice is it, but how was it earned? Tradition says Bhago was shaken, and changed his ways.
screen: `FROM LALO'S BREAD, MILK.` · `FROM BHAGO'S FEAST, BLOOD.` · `MIRACLE OR PARABLE: SIKHS READ BOTH.` · `FOOD CARRIES ITS HISTORY.` · then, large: `HOW WAS IT EARNED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think where one thing you own came from. Settle. Pick something near you: your shoes, your phone, the chair. Now trace it back as far as you can. Who made it? Where? Who carried it? Who was paid, and who maybe wasn't? You won't know all of it. That's fine. Just follow it as far as you can, without guilt and without a verdict. The bell holds the time.
Milk and blood. Tradition's picture of honest bread and stolen wealth, pressed in Guru Nanak's hands. Today's word.
Your line: how was it earned. Today, ask it once about something you're about to buy, and once about something you're about to earn. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the milk-and-blood sakhi as a teaching about honest earnings; many gurdwaras and families use it to explain why kirat, honest work, matters, and some Sikhs give a tenth of their income, dasvandh, from earnings made honestly.

fork.setup: you're Malik Bhago. the Guru has just pressed your fine food and blood has run out of it, in front of the whole town. what do you do?
options: laugh it off as a trick.
take it to heart and change your ways.
fork.reveal: tradition says Bhago was shaken and changed. the story isn't about ruining him; it's about letting him see.

original.note: Gurmukhi: hakk, what rightfully belongs to someone, from Arabic haqq; the word in Nanak's line about another's due.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with bread.
what it means: food carries its history. honest bread nourishes like milk; wealth squeezed from the poor is, in the story's picture, their blood.
what a scholar hears: a janamsakhi wonder, not in the scripture, built on a real hymn that likens taking another's due to pork for a Muslim and beef for a Hindu.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi traditions (milk from Lalo's bread, blood from Bhago's food)

notes: The salok 'hakk paraaiaa naanakaa us sooar us gaai' is placed in Var Majh at Ang 141; confirm Ang and paraphrase.
The milk-and-blood episode is absent from some early janamsakhis and prominent in later tradition; the script says only that it comes from 'the later life stories' and not the scripture. Confirm.
Two readings (literal miracle, parable) presented without ranking; confirm acceptable.
Bhago changing his ways is tradition; confirm.
